 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

   

   

 Supreme Court Appeal Numbers: S:AP:IE:2025:0000064 (Redwood) 

             S:AP:IE:2025:0000065 (Nua) 

 [2026] IESC 3 

   

   

   

 O'Donnell CJ 

 Dunne J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Murray J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

   

 BETWEEN/ 

   

 REDWOOD EXTENDED CARE FACILITY 

   

                                                                         APPELLANT/RESPONDENT 

   

  AND  

   

 TAILTE ÉIREANN (FORMERLY THE COMMISSIONER FOR VALUATION) 

   

 RESPONDENT/APPELLANT 

   

   

 and 

   

   

   

 BETWEEN/ 

   

 NUA HEALTHCARE SERVICES LIMITED 

   

                                                                         APPELLANT/RESPONDENT 

   

  AND  

   

 TAILTE ÉIREANN (FORMERLY THE COMMISSIONER FOR VALUATION) 

   

 RESPONDENT/APPELLANT 

 

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Brian Murray delivered this 28 th day of January 2026 

 

 

 1.       Schedule 4, paragraph 14 of the Valuation Act 2001 (" para. 14 ") refers to: 

   

 ' 14.Any land, building or part of a building occupied for the purpose of caring for elderly, handicapped or disabled persons by a body, being either 

   

 (a) a body which is not established and the affairs of which are not conducted for the purpose of making a private profit from an activity as aforesaid, or 

   

 (b) a body the expenses incurred by which in carrying on an activity as aforesaid are defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer , other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the Nursing Homes Support Scheme Act 2009. ' 

   

 (emphasis added) 

      

 2.       The effect of s. 15(2) of that statute (" the 2001 Act ") is that if a property falls within this description, it is not rateable.  The issue in this appeal is whether para. 14(b) captures certain care facilities owned and operated by Redwood Extended Care Facility and Nua Healthcare Services Limited (" Redwood ", " Nua " and, collectively, " the respondents ").                                                                                                                                                                               

   

 3.       Essentially, the respondents say that all, or nearly all, of the expenses incurred by them in providing care facilities of the kind mentioned in para. 14 from the properties in question are discharged from monies paid to them by the Health Services Executive (" HSE ") or (in the case of Nua), the HSE and TUSLA, that those monies are paid to the respondents as the providers to HSE and TUSLA of services involving the care of particular persons, that the expenses are accordingly defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer, and that the properties at which those services are provided are thus exempt from rates.  Tailte Éireann (" TE ") disagrees, contending that the HSE and TUSLA do not ' defray ' those expenses where they make payments to the respondents under service arrangements.  TE contends that the ordinary meaning of ' defrayal ' in this statutory context entails the assessment of vouched expenses and their reimbursement or payment.  In order to ' defray ' those costs, it suggests, HSE and TUSLA would have to receive, vouch and remit the vouched sum to the respondents.  This they do not do.  

   

 4.       By decisions of 27 October 2021 (Redwood) and 6 May 2022 (Nua) the Valuation Tribunal (" the Tribunal ") determined that the properties were exempt.  On appeal by way of case stated, the High Court agreed ( [2025] IEHC 197 ).  This Court [2025] IESCDET 90 ( Redwood ) and [2025] IESCDET 89 ( Nua ) granted TE leave to appeal the decision of the High Court, considering that the appeal met the threshold of exceptional circumstances warranting an appeal directly from the High Court.  The question of general importance arising was the proper interpretation of the exemption provided for in para. 14(b), and in particular whether that exemption applies where the HSE enters into a Service Level Agreement with a service provider, only making payments relating to service users who might be present from to time. A similar issue arises in respect of the arrangements between Nua and TUSLA.  The answers to those questions depend on whether the fact that expenses of a facility of the kind referred in para. 14(b) are incorporated into and discharged from the contract price paid by the HSE or TUSLA to the respondents in consideration for the services the respondents provide at the request of those statutory bodies, means that those expenses are ' defrayed ... out of moneys provided by the Exchequer '. 

   

 ***** 

   

 5.       Redwood operates a designated centre (a term defined in the s. 2 of the Health Act 2007 as including an institution at which certain residential services are provided by the HSE or a service provider under that Act) .  It caters for adults with intellectual disabilities and/or acquired brain injuries. It provides that service from a property owned by it on the outskirts of Stamullen, Co. Meath. The property comprises a six-bedroomed, two-storey detached premises. Five of these bedrooms are occupied by adults availing of those care facilities. The premises is operated under a written service agreement (described on its face as an " Service Arrangement ") with the HSE.  That Arrangement comes in two parts.  Part 1, ' Standard Clauses ', includes the terms and conditions under which the HSE funds Redwood for care services.  Part 2 consists of various service schedules which are furnished by each HSE Community Healthcare Organisation and are returned in respect of each resident funded by the HSE. 

   

 6.       Until the events giving rise to this appeal, the property was not rated.  An application having been made for a revision of valuation following a request by Meath County Council, the revision officer determined that a material change of circumstances had occurred within the meaning of s. 3 of the 2001 Act.  Following the making of representations by Redwood, on 23 August 2018 a final valuation certificate was issued for the property, recording a valuation of  56.  Redwood appealed this valuation to the Tribunal. 

   

 7.       Nua similarly owns a designated care facility.  That facility is registered pursuant to SI No. 366 of 2013, the Health Act 2007 (Registration of Designated Centres for Persons (Children and Adults) with Disabilities Regulations 2013.  It is subject to the regulatory conditions specified in SI No. 367/2013, the Health Act 2007 (Care and Support of Residents in Designated Centres for Persons (Children and Adults) with Disabilities) Regulations 2013.  The facility acts as a supported residence for the provision of 24-hour care to four children aged between 12 and 18.  The children have a wide range of support needs including autism, intellectual disability and challenging behaviours.  The facility is at a property located in Kiltinan, Co. Tipperary.  That property (" Millview ") comprises a five-bedroomed dormer bungalow on a site of approximately 0.22 hectares.  It is leased by Maple Healthcare Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Nua.  The facility is also operated under a Service Arrangement entered into between Nua and the HSE.  This Arrangement is similar to that in place with Redwood.  There is no equivalent written contract with TUSLA, which places some of the children housed by Nua.  The agreement with TUSLA comes in the form of a costing proposal for individual children admitted to Nua's care. 

   

 8.       Millview was not rated before the events giving rise to this appeal.  On 8 October 2018, Nua was issued a final valuation certificate for the property pursuant to s. 24(1) of the 2001 Act, recording a valuation of 41 per sqm. Nua appealed this valuation to the Tribunal. 

   

 ***** 

   

 9.       The 2001 Act  the first comprehensive valuation legislation since the 1850s - overhauled valuation law in the State, replacing a cumbersome and largely Victorian, rating code.  The central principle is now stated in s. 15(1): all ' relevant property ' is rateable, the adjective ' rateable ' meaning that it is property in respect of which a rate may be made (s. 14(1)).  Relevant property is defined by reference to the Third Schedule to the Act, which lists 14 species of property, and specifies one condition to the exemption.  The condition is that the property concerned is occupied and the nature of that occupation is such as to constitute rateable occupation of the property.  Rateable occupation, in turn, is defined by reference to the law in force prior to the enactment of the legislation. 

   

 10.   Section 15(2) of the 2001 Act provides that ' relevant property ' referred to in Schedule 4 is not rateable.  For present purposes, the properties iterated in Schedule 4 can be separated into four categories.  First, there are properties defined simply by reference to a particular use (agricultural land, land developed for horticulture, forestry or sport, farm buildings, certain domestic premises, property used exclusively for public religious worship, community halls, turf bogs or turf banks used for the purposes of cutting or making turf mould).  Second, there are properties defined by reference to a specific use and subject to a condition that (to paraphrase) the body occupying it is established or the activity is undertaken, otherwise than for profit (the precise expression varies from paragraph to paragraph).  This is how premises used for community sport, burial grounds, certain cultural institutions and places of recreation that are open to the public, properties occupied by societies established for the advancement of science, literature or the fine arts and used exclusively for that purpose, properties occupied by charitable organisations and used for charitable purposes and properties used for the provision of early childhood care and education, are addressed.  Third, there are properties that are exempt from rates simply by reason of being owned by specific named bodies (including certain specified bodies that own or operate cultural institutions, Departments of State, the Defence Forces or An Garda Síochána, certain elected representatives or the HSE). 

   

 11.   Fourth, and most importantly for present purposes, there are three species of exempt properties that are defined by reference to use, and that must meet either a condition that the body using the property is not established and its affairs are not conducted for the purpose of making a private profit or that its expenses are ' defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer '.  These properties must be ' used by a body for the purposes of caring for sick persons, for the treatment of illnesses or as a maternity hospital ' (para. 8), be occupied by certain educational institutions and ' used exclusively by [them] for the provision of the educational services ... and otherwise than for private profit, being a school, college, university, institute of technology or other educational institution ' (para. 10) or be ' occupied for the purpose of caring for elderly, handicapped or disabled persons ' (para. 14).  It might be noted that the general exemption expressed for properties occupied by the HSE (para. 20) excludes properties referred to at paras. 8 and 14: 

   

 ' Any land, building or part of a building occupied by the Health Service Executive other than any land, building or part of a building referred to in paragraph 8 or 14. ' 

   

   

 12.   The language appearing in para. 14(b) and around which the issues in this appeal revolve ( ' defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer ') was introduced for the first time in the 2001 Act and does not appear to have any analogue in other common law jurisdictions.  The decision of the High Court in Glendale Nursing Home v. Commissioner of Valuation [2012] IEHC 254 (" Glendale ") is the only decision of the courts  before the judgment of Bradley J. the subject of this appeal - in which the meaning of the provision has been canvassed.  It featured prominently in the decisions of the Tribunal and the High Court giving rise to this appeal to the extent that an understanding of those decisions depends on an appreciation of the issue before the Court in Glendale .  Indeed the decision in that case prompted an amendment to para. 14(b) that is of importance in construing the provision as it stands today. 

   

 ***** 

   

 13.   In Glendale , the Court (Birmingham J., as he then was) was concerned with an earlier iteration of para. 14(b) which omitted the words ' other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the Nursing Homes Support Scheme Act 2009 ' (these words were subsequently inserted by the Valuation (Amendment) Act 2015).  The appellant owned and operated a nursing home.  It contended that it fell within para. 14(b) as it then stood as more than 50% of its income was derived from a Nursing Home Subvention Scheme and a Nursing Home Support Scheme paid (respectively) by the HSE in compliance with the provisions of the Health (Nursing Homes) (Amendment) Act 2007 and the Nursing Homes Support Scheme Act 2009 (" the 2009 Act ").  The Nursing Home Subvention Scheme was introduced in 1993 and was replaced by the Nursing Homes Support Scheme (or ' Fair Deal ' as it became widely known).  Upon the introduction of the Nursing Homes Support Scheme, no new entrants were admitted to the Subvention Scheme (although those already on that scheme could elect to remain on it, or to transfer to the new scheme).  That said, the issue in the case (as described by Birmingham J. at para. 2 of his judgment) was inter alia , whether the HSE in making payments to nursing homes under the 2009 Act was ' within the ordinary meaning of the word, defraying the expenses of the nursing home in its purpose of caring for the elderly '. 

   

 14.   The Valuation Tribunal in Glendale had concluded that the HSE, in making payments to nursing homes under the 2009 Act, was ' defraying ' expenses of those nursing homes, but it was not satisfied on the evidence before it that Glendale's expenses were defrayed ' wholly or mainly ' out of monies provided by the Exchequer.  That finding was made in a context in which under the Nursing Homes Support Scheme, the individual in need of care made a contribution towards the cost of their care, and the State paid the balance irrespective of whether the nursing home was public, private or voluntary, in which the application was made by the individual availing of that care, and in which that individual chose the particular nursing home at which they received it.  If the individual selected a public nursing home, they paid their contribution to the HSE, and if they chose a voluntary nursing home or private nursing home, they paid their contribution each week and the HSE paid the balance.  In certain circumstances, the HSE could recoup some of the monies it expended on behalf of persons admitted to nursing homes. 

   

 15.   Those features of the legal regime caused Birmingham J. to conclude that the focus of the provision of both State support and subvention was on the individual in need of care rather than the care provider. He said (at para. 19) that the State through the HSE ' has sought to ... offer support and assistance to those requiring care rather than setting out with the objective of assisting private or voluntary care providers .' In reaching that conclusion the judge was particularly struck by the fact that it was possible under the Support Scheme to enter a nursing home in Northern Ireland. 

   

 16.   In the course of his judgment, Birmingham J. addressed the meaning of the word ' defray '.  He approved the decision of the Valuation Tribunal that the ordinary meaning of this term was ' to discharge (the expense or cost of anything, by payment) '.  In construing the word, he said, it was important to focus not just on the term, but on the context in which it appeared.  He said (para. 24): 

   

 ' In that regard it is worth noting that para 14(b) is couched in the passive tense.  That being so, the question is not whether the State/HSE intended to support Glendale by defraying its expenses or still less whether that was the primary motivation of the State/HSE, but whether that is what in fact happened, i.e., whether it can legitimately be said that the expenses of Glendale are being defrayed by the HSE. '     

   

 17.   Having observed that this would be a ' wholly strained, contrived and artificial use of language ', Birmingham J. continued (paras. 26-28): 

   

 26. Over and above what the HSE intends to do, what it is actually doing is contributing to the cost of care for the individual elderly person, alleviating the burden on the elderly person in obtaining care.  It might be said that the State/HSE defrays the expenses of the individual elderly person in need of care but it cannot be said that they are defraying the costs of Glendale. 

   

 27. If a delicatessen draws its clientele to a significant extent from amongst the ranks of public servants, could it seriously be said that the State, as pay master of the public servants, was defraying the expenses of the delicatessen?  If an adjoining cafe is frequented by employees of a large company that provides its employees with luncheon vouchers redeemable at various locations across the city, could it be said that the employer in providing the vouchers which were used in the cafe was defraying the costs and expenses of that cafe?  If a public house draws its clientele from the students of a third level college who are in receipt of grant cheques from the Department of Education could it be said that the expenses of the public house are being defrayed by the Department? 

   

 28. I am not at all convinced that it could ever be said that the State, by agreeing to offer financial support or subvention to individual elderly people in need of care, could be said to be defraying the expenses of Glendale.  I have already pointed out that individuals are entitled to opt for a nursing home in Northern Ireland.  On that basis can it be said that the expenses of Northern Ireland nursing homes are being defrayed by the HSE? ' 

   

 ***** 

   

 18.   The evidence tendered on behalf of Redwood to the Tribunal was to the effect that all five places at the facility were filled by the HSE.  Redwood, it was said, pays for the full costs of the house, the full running of the house, including light and heat, food, petrol for a car used in connection with the services provided there, the car itself and any costs associated with the house.  The evidence before the Tribunal was that Redwood carried out an assessment on individuals at the request of the HSE, with a view to determining if they are suitable for the house and whether Redwood deems that it can provide a service and an appropriate home for them.  If so, Redwood engages with the HSE setting out the full costs and agreeing a level of funding required to cover the costs of caring for that person.  If the person is admitted to the home, Redwood then invoices the HSE on a monthly basis, those invoices reflecting the care needs and fees incurred by Redwood in respect of each person cared for.  The payments made on foot of those invoices, it was said, represented the sole source of funds to Redwood and its only income.  What the HSE paid, it was said, was a sum reflecting the cost to Redwood of providing the service in question, plus profit.  The evidence was that as part of the tendering process with the HSE, the proposed breakdown of fees, which included a profit margin, were fully disclosed to the HSE. 

   

 19.   From there, the following facts were either found by the Tribunal, or not disputed: 

   

 (i)                  Redwood was established for profit. 

   

 (ii)               The property is occupied for the purpose of caring for disabled persons who have intellectual difficulties. 

   

 (iii)             The funding received by Redwood from the HSE represented Redwood's sole and exclusive revenue stream. 

   

 (iv)              That funding did not arise under the 2009 Act and therefore there was no defrayal of expenses under that Act, being ' a different model entirely '. 

   

 (v)                The residents of the property were placed by the HSE on foot of Service Level Agreements between the HSE and Redwood whereby it was agreed to provide accommodation, food and support services to the service user at an agreed rate.  Invoices were then raised to reflect the care needs and fees incurred by Redwood in respect of each service user for whom they cared. 

   

 (vi)              The HSE provided money to Redwood qua service provider. 

   

 20.   In its written determination, the Tribunal noted that in order to avail of the exemption provided for in para. 14, Redwood was bound to establish that the exemption applies clearly and without doubt, and in express terms, citing the judgment of MacMenamin J. in Nangles Nurseries v. Commissioners for Valuation [2008] IEHC 73 (" Nangles Nurseries ").  It said that Redwood received 100% of its expenses and income from the HSE (it said that ' the Exchequer ' referred to in para. 14(b) ' refers to and incorporates the HSE ').  It expressed the view that it was not clear that the fact that Redwood derived a profit from its dealings with the HSE is conclusive or supportive of the argument for excluding Redwood from the exemption.  Noting the provisions of paragraph 14(a), the Tribunal expressed the view that two eventualities were envisaged by the provision: one for profit and the other not for profit. Later, it explained that para. 14(a) covers non-profit entities and para. 14(b) for-profit entities.   It said of Redwood ' its income is its expenses and this is the cost of operating '.  It noted paragraph 4.1 of the Service Level Agreement between Redwood and the HSE, which said ' the funds to be paid by the Executive to the Provider inclusive of all duties, taxes, expenses and other costs associated with or incurred in the provision of the Services shall not exceed the amount specified in Schedule 6 (Funding)... '. 

   

 21.   The Tribunal found that there was no defrayal by the HSE of the expenses of individual service users, and that Redwood was provided with monies from which it defrayed the expenses of carrying out its activities.  The difference between these was relevant to the Tribunal's analysis of the decision in Glendale. That case, it said, was concerned with a ' sufficiently distinct ' scenario, and cannot be taken as applying outside the nursing home setting.  It stressed that in the present case, the service user has limited autonomy over where they are placed and that under the ' Fair Deal ' scheme, there was a ' top up ' facility while in the present case, Redwood received 100% of its funding from the HSE with no additional funds sought from the service users.  The Glendale decision, it said, was of limited assistance because of the distinguishing features of the statutory scheme that applied to the property occupied by the appellant in that case.  They did not, the Tribunal found, cross over to the non-nursing home setting. 

   

 22.   The Tribunal concluded that the relevant property fell within the ambit of para. 14(b). It held that Redwood was a body the expenses incurred by which in carrying on an activity of caring for disabled persons are defrayed by the Exchequer, other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the 2009 Act.  The Tribunal allowed the appeal and decreased the valuation of the property to 0 . 

   

 23.   An appeal to the High Court lies against decisions of the Tribunal on a point of law by way of case stated.  This is provided for in s. 39 of the 2001 Act.  The Tribunal in accordance with the procedure stipulated there, identified the following three questions of law in the case stated by it for the opinion of the High Court: 

   

 1.       Having regard to the evidence before it, did the Tribunal err in law in determining that the relevant property fell within the ambit of paragraph 14(b), Schedule 4 of the Valuation Act 2001, as amended? 

   

 2.        Did the Tribunal err in law in its interpretation of the term "defrayal of expenses"? Specifically, did the Tribunal err in law in determining that where the payments are calculated on the costs of the service users, and only paid relating to any person who might be present from time to time, that nonetheless amounts to a defrayal of the Appellant's expenses, as opposed to income, contrary to the decision in Glendale? 

   

 3.       Did the Tribunal err in law in determining that a body carrying on an activity for profit was entitled to avail of the exemption applied? 

   

 24.   Before the High Court, the parties agreed that the third question was not being pursued. 

   

 ***** 

   

 25.   The Tribunal in Nua's appeal identified three questions as arising from the applicability of para. 14(b) to the property - (a) whether the HSE/the Exchequer provides funds to Nua qua service provider, or whether it provides them to the service users cared for by Nua, (b) whether and to what extent the expenses incurred by Nua in carrying on that activity are defrayed wholly or mainly out of monies provided by the Exchequer, and (c) whether and to what extent the decision in Glendale applies to this case. 

   

 26.    The evidence tendered on behalf of Nua was to the effect that residents are referred from the HSE or by the courts through TUSLA.  The admissions process involves a bed space demand and needs assessment as well as a review of the peer-to-peer impact on existing residents.  A cost proposal is then forwarded to the courts or the HSE which includes Nua's view of the level of likely care required.  If the proposal is accepted, a further assessment is made by Nua and a costing proposal prepared in accordance with an existing Service Level Agreement between Nua and the HSE. 

   

 27.   Against that background, the following facts were either found by the Tribunal, or not disputed: 

   

 (i)                  The property was not a nursing home for the purposes of para. 14 and there was no defrayal of expenses under the Nursing Home Support Scheme Act 2009. 

   

 (ii)               The subject property was profit-making and was owned by Nua.  Therefore, it said, there was no defrayal of expenses under the 2009 Act. 

   

 (iii)             The designated care centre operated under a HSE service agreement and a costing proposal agreement with TUSLA. 

   

 (iv)              In 2019, 97.8% of all monies received by Nua came from the HSE and TUSLA, and in 2019, 100% of the income received in Millview was entirely from these entities. 

   

 (v)                There was no direct agreement between Nua and individual residents and individual residents were not party to any costing proposal arrangements. 

   

 (vi)              Each month Nua invoiced the HSE for the total cost of providing residential care, community outreach and day services.  Invoices were not issued to and were not copied to individual residents or their families. 

   

 28.   As in Redwood, the Tribunal found that the facts were distinguishable from those in Glendale.  That case, the Tribunal stressed, related to the Nursing Home Support Scheme, and the Tribunal found as a fact that Millview was not a nursing home.  The 2009 Act set out prescriptive and extensive provisions regarding the Fair Deal scheme.  The National Treatment Purchase Fund negotiates the price under the Nursing Home Support Scheme Act and that differs from the pricing process for the care provision of service users in this case.  In Glendale, the HSE payments were made in respect of a shortfall charged by the nursing home to the consumer and the person in receipt of care may be required to ' top up ' the contribution if they elected for a private nursing home.   There was no ' top up ' involved in the payments agreed between the HSE and Nua, and no question of monies being recouped by the HSE/the State from those receiving care: ' [i]n the present case ... the service is delivered on behalf of the State, in circumstances where the State is not delivering this service directly ' (para. 10.12 of the Tribunal's judgment). 

   

 29.   Based on the evidence it heard and documents it had considered, the Tribunal concluded in its written determination that the HSE and TUSLA were providing funds to Nua as a service provider as that term is used in s. 2 of the Health Act 2007.  In reaching that conclusion it attached significance to the fact that individual residents are not party to any costing agreements, to the fact that Nua invoiced the HSE each month for the total cost of providing residential care, community outreach and day services, and to the uncontradicted evidence that it would be in breach of Regulation 24 of SI No. 367/2013 if any of the residents' own funds were used to defray the expense of their care in Millview.  It said the following (at para. 10.21): 

   

 '... the Tribunal finds that there is no defrayal by the HSE of the expenses of the Service Users in the present case and that the Appellant is provided with monies from which they defray the expenses of carrying out the activity. ' 

   

 30.   Having regard to the foregoing, the Tribunal determined that the property fell within the ambit of the exemption provided for in para. 14(b). It found that Nua was a body the expenses incurred by which in carrying on an activity of caring for disabled persons were defrayed by the Exchequer, other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the 2009 Act. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and decreased the valuation of the property to 0. 

   

 31.   The Tribunal - in accordance with the appeal procedure provided for in s. 39 of the 2001 Act - identified the following five questions of law in the case stated by the Tribunal for the opinion of the High Court: 

   

 1.       Having regard to the evidence before it, did the Tribunal err in law in determining that the relevant property fell within the ambit of the exemption provided for at paragraph 14(b), schedule 4 of the Valuation Acts 2001 to 2015? 

   

 2.       Did the Tribunal err in law and/or in fact in determining that the HSE and TUSLA provided funds to the Appellant as a service provider rather than providing the funds to the service users cared for by the Appellant? 

   

 3.       Did the Tribunal err in law and/or in fact in holding that there was no defrayal by the HSE of the expenses of the service users in the present case and that the Appellant was provided with monies from which it defrayed the expenses of carrying out its activities? 

   

 4.       Did the Tribunal err in law and/or in fact in determining that the expenses incurred by the Appellant in carrying on its activities were defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer? 

   

 5.       Did the Tribunal err in law in its interpretation and application of the decision of the High Court in Glendale Nursing Home v. The Commissioner of Valuation [2012] IEHC 254 to the present case? 

   

   

 32.   Before the High Court, the parties agreed that the second of these questions was no longer being pursued. 

   

 ***** 

   

 33.   Bradley J. delivered one judgment in respect of both appeals. He described the issue of statutory interpretation common to each of the two appeals as ' quite net ', stating that ultimately it could be said to come down to the interpretation of the four words ' out of moneys provided ' in para. 14(b).  In resolving that issue, he reasoned as follows: 

   

 (i)                  He did not consider that there was any ambiguity in the provisions of paras. 14(a) and (b) of Schedule 4, or in the use of the words ' expenses ' or ' defrayment '.   The reference to ' expenses ' is to the expenses incurred in carrying on an activity and that ' defrayment ' is as referred to in Glendale , ' payment '.  He stated that it was common case between the parties that the use of the word ' Exchequer ' in these provisions is synonymous with the ' HSE ' (para. 80). 

   

 (ii)               That being so, he was of the view that the position of the Commissioner did not accord with what he considered to be the correct interpretation of paras. 14(a) or (b) (para. 82). 

   

 (iii)             Bradley J. stressed that the Tribunal did not find that there was a defrayal by the HSE or TUSLA of the expenses of the respondents.  Rather, it found that they both received payments from the HSE or TUSLA in return for services across a number of centres and that from that income, the respondents defrayed the expenses of carrying out its activity (para. 89). 

   

 (iv)              He distinguished the decision in Glendale on the basis that the Fair Deal Scheme provided a contribution towards the cost of an individual's care based on the individual's financial means at the time of application.  What the State was doing was providing support to individuals as a service user and not to the service provider.  In the case of the respondents, HSE pays all the moneys used in the care of the patients to the patient's provider and they defray their expenses out of those monies (paras. 92 and 121). 

   

 (v)                In that regard, Bradley J. again stressed that in the case of the respondents, the HSE was entering into a contractual arrangement with a service provider under a Service Level Arrangement to fund all of the costs associated with or incurred in the provision of residential and specialist care services for the purpose of caring for elderly, handicapped or disabled persons (para. 115).  The costings covered a range of matters in the provision of an individual's accommodation, health and social care needs and these ' are wholly defrayed out of moneys provided by the HSE' (para. 116). 

   

 34.   Bradley J. expressed his conclusion, as follows (at para. 121): 

   

 ' ...the Fair Deal Scheme which was the central issue in Glendale provided a contribution towards the cost of an individual's care based on the persons financial means at the time of application. In Glendale, the court found, in the context of a nursing home, that what the State was doing was providing support to individuals as a service user and not to the service provider (and Nua and Redwood are service providers). In the case of Redwood and Nua, the Exchequer (HSE) pays all the moneys used in the care of the patients to the patient's provider and they defray their expenses out of those moneys whereas in Glendale the focus was on the patient and the statutory provisions of the Fair Deal Scheme. In the Redwood case, for example, the Valuation Tribunal found (at paragraph 8.3) that all of the money was provided to Redwood by the Exchequer and that any expenses incurred by Redwood in connection with their activities were paid or defrayed out of the money that comes in from the HSE. This finding was also subtended, for example, in the evidence adduced by Mr. O'Toole under questioning from counsel for Redwood. In the context of the nature of the appeal before me, this and the other evidence (including documentary evidence) led to a finding of the Tribunal based on the evidence before it. ' 

   

   

 ***** 

   

 35.   It has long been legislative policy in Ireland that properties used for some public and charitable purposes - and in particular certain properties dedicated to religious purposes, or properties used for the provision of educational and medical services other than for profit - should be exempt from rates.  At the time of the enactment of the 2001 Act, that category of exemption was governed by a proviso in s. 63 of the Poor Relief (Ireland) Act, 1838 (" the 1838 Act "), and this provision had since the 1860s been understood as the critical reference point for identifying exemptions from rateability ( Londonderry Union (Guardians) v. Londonderry Bridge Commissioners (1868) IR 2 CL 577).  It read: 

   

 ' Provided also, that no church, chapel, or other building exclusively dedicated to religious worship, or exclusively used for the education of the poor, nor any burial ground or cemetery, nor any infirmary, hospital, charity school or other building used exclusively for charitable purposes, nor any building, land or hereditament dedicated to or used for public purposes, shall be rateable, except where any private profit or use shall be directly derived therefrom, in which case the person deriving such profit or use shall be liable to be rated as an occupier according to the annual value of such profit or use ' . 

   

   

 36.   The fact that this provision (rather than the provisions in later legislation, s. 2 of the Valuation (Ireland) Act 1854) was found to govern exemptions from rating in this jurisdiction resulted in Irish law significantly deviating from that in England, where it was only property in the actual occupation of the government or its servants that benefitted from a public purposes exemption ( Mersey Docks and Harbour Board Trustees v. Cameron (1865) 11 H.L. Cas. 443).  In Ireland, the application of the public purpose component of exemption (as opposed to the charitable aspect) broadly speaking depended upon whether the property was operated for the benefit of the public generally, emphasis being placed on whether it was established by statute, accountable to parliament and subject to public audit.  This resulted in some fine distinctions, exemplified by the holding that while University College Cork was exempt ( University College Cork v. Commissioner of Valuation [1912] 2 IR 328), neither Trinity College Dublin ( Trinity College v. Commissioner of Valuation [1919] 2 IR 493) nor Maynooth College ( Maynooth College v. Commissioner of Valuation [1958] IR 189), enjoyed that privilege.  Misfortune, Davitt P. memorably observed in the latter case, made for strange bedfellows (at p. 203). 

   

 37.   Properties dedicated to, or used for, public purposes were thus understood to comprise those owned by the government, or those in which it could be said that each member of the public enjoyed an interest (see in particular the judgment of Keane CJ in Port of Cork Company v. Commissioner of Valuation [2004] 1 ILRM 151 , 156).  While s. 63 of the 1838 Act made it clear that the public purposes proviso was applicable ' except where any private profit or use shall be directly derived therefrom ', the position in relation to charitable bodies was more nuanced.  In Barrington's Hospital v. Commissioner of Valuation [1957] IR 299, the former Supreme Court held that a public voluntary hospital was charitable in purpose under s. 63 of the 1838 Act despite the fact that some of its in-patients were private patients paying full hospital charges.  A purpose, Kingsmill Moore J. said, was no less charitable if the care was not given gratuitously, provided that the institution in or by which it is afforded is not so conducted as to show habitually a surplus of receipts over expenditure (p. 324). Even if there were a small net profit from private patients, this would not prevent the voluntary hospital in issue there from being used ' exclusively for charitable purposes ' if the profit was subject to an obligation to apply it to the general purposes of the hospital (at p. 335). 

   

 38.   Part of the overhaul of the system of valuation effected by the 2001 Act involved a reorientation of the public purposes exemption, with s. 8 of that Act repealing s. 63 of the 1838 Act.  For present purposes, two components of the new regime are relevant.  First, under s. 15(3) of the 2001 Act as enacted relevant property was not rateable if directly occupied by ' the State ' (as explained later, this provision was subsequently repealed and replaced in part by a new paragraph in Schedule 4 of the 2001 Act).  This was non-exhaustively defined as including property ' occupied by any Department or office of State, the Defence Forces or the Garda Síochána or used as a prison or place of detention '.  Second, as I have earlier noted, included in the relevant properties that were not rateable listed in Schedule 4 were certain properties that had previously been brought within s. 63 of the 1838 Act, including those used for public religious worship, for the caring for the sick or infirm, certain educational institutions, burial grounds and cemeteries.  Some of the language used in s. 63 of the 1838 Act made its way back into Schedule 4, including the terms used ' exclusively for charitable purposes ' and ' private profit '.   As I have also noted, that Schedule defined some of these exemptions solely by use, some by use but subject to a condition that the body is established or activity undertaken otherwise than for profit, some by the identity of the owner and three   of which paragraph 14 is one - by use and a condition that the property not be established and its affairs not conducted for the purpose of making a private profit, or that its expenses ' are defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer '. 

   

 39.   The relationship between the exemptions from rates and the provision of health services came to the fore early in the history of the 2001 Act.  In HSE v. Commissioner of Valuation [2008] IEHC 178 ; [2010] 4 IR 23 the question was whether administrative offices owned and operated by the HSE were outside the rating net.   The HSE contended that they were, arguing that it was ' the State ' or ' an office of State ' within the meaning of s. 15(3) as enacted. Counsel for the Commissioner suggested that paras. 8 and 14 of Schedule 4 exhaustively defined the categories of exemption of HSE owned properties (see para. 16 of the judgment).  The High Court rejected that argument, holding that having regard to inter alia its close proximity with central government and its role in the provision of health services - a core function, it was found, of ' the State ' - the HSE was ' the State ' (but not, as the Tribunal had found, ' an office of State ').  An appeal to this Court by the Commissioner was subsequently withdrawn, and subsequent legislative developments render the question of whether the conclusion reached by the High Court was correct, academic.  But the proposition subtending the Commissioner's argument, when viewed in the light of the state of the law governing exemptions from rating when the 2001 Act was enacted, provides a good starting point for understanding what the Oireachtas was seeking to achieve in the formulation it employed in paras. 8 and 14. 

   

 40.   Noting that the establishment of the HSE (which was effected by the Health Act 2004 (" the 2004 Act ")) post-dated the 2001 Act (the 2004 Act transferred to the HSE functions of the health boards established under the Health Act 1970),  it is clear that these provisions combined to exempt from rates medical facilities occupied by the HSE and from which it provided services to the community in discharge of its statutory remit and obligations.  Like the former Health Boards, the HSE was not established for the purposes of making a profit from the activity of providing those services and it is hard to see that any profit that it happened to make in respect of a particular activity could ever be said to be ' private '.  Therefore, paras. 8(a) and 14(a) exclude HSE owned medical facilities from the rating process.  Moreover, the effect of para. 16 of Schedule 4 when viewed in the light of the decision in Barrington's Hospital v. Commissioner of Valuation , would be to exempt at least some such properties where owned by charitable organisations, even if some of the activities were conducted for the purposes of making a profit (' [a]ny land ... occupied by a body, being ... a charitable organisation that uses the land, building or part exclusively for charitable purposes and otherwise than for private profit '). 

   

 41.   This suggests an underlying, albeit general, policy that agencies providing medical and cognate care facilities should not pay rates when doing so for what would have been described in the pre-existing law as public or charitable purposes.  If paras. 8 and 14 of Schedule 4 had stopped at (a), however, that might have created an anomaly.  It is clear that the HSE has the power to subcontract the provision of the services it is obligated by statute to make available (as indeed did the Health Boards - see s. 26 of the Health Act 1970).  Logically, if the HSE is exempted from a rates liability where it provides such services from a premises, it might be thought that it should not have to pay those same rates as part of the price of subcontracting the same services.  Where the greater part of the business of private bodies involved the provision of those services, it might be said to have made little sense that the HSE - which was intended to be exempt from rates where providing these services itself - would end up paying those rates indirectly as part of the consideration it paid for provision of these services.  Accordingly, if the Oireachtas had decided that properties occupied by the HSE from which it discharged its statutory obligations in the provision of medical or cognate care should be exempt from rates, there was a logic to also exempting those properties from which private undertakings provided the same services for the HSE.  Thus, it happened that a very significant change in the law governing exemptions for medical and some other care facilities was effected by Schedule 4, with paras. 8(b) and 14(b) enabling bodies operating such premises to both avail of an exemption from rates, and to make a private profit from that activity. 

   

 42.   That paras. 8 and 14 were designed with the Health Boards specifically in mind is shown by what happened following the decision in HSE v. Commissioner of Valuation (and for that matter a number of other cases before the Tribunal and the High Court in which various other statutory bodies had argued on the back of that decision that they also comprised ' the State ' for the purposes of s. 15(3)).   Section 15(3) was repealed by the Local Government Reform Act 2014, which at the same time inserted a para. 12A into Schedule 4 the effect of which was to exempt property directly occupied by ' any Department or Office of State ' (as well as property occupied by the Defence Forces and An Garda Síochána or places of detention).  The Health Service Executive (Financial Matters) Act 2014 then inserted a para. 20 into the same Schedule exempting ' [a]ny land, building or part of a building occupied by the Health Service Executive other than any land, building or part of a building referred to in paragraph 8 or 14' . 

   

 *****   

 43.   The rationale I have suggested for para. 14(b) (that the HSE should not find itself indirectly paying rates for a property at which a service the HSE has contracted out is provided if the HSE is exempted from a rates liability were it providing those services from the premises itself) fits readily within the language of the provision. It is helpful to quote it again: 

   

 ' 14.Any land, building or part of a building occupied for the purpose of caring for elderly, handicapped or disabled persons by a body, being... 

   

 ... 

   

 (b) a body the expenses incurred by which in carrying on an activity as aforesaid are defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys provided by the Exchequer , other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the Nursing Homes Support Scheme Act 2009. ' 

   

 (emphasis added) 

   

 44.   There can, I think, be no doubt but that viewing this provision literally and in the abstract, the respondents fall within its terms.  As I have earlier noted, each property is a ' designated centre ' for the purposes of s. 2 of the Health Act 2007.   Each property is occupied for the purpose of caring for ... disabled persons '.  The respondents conduct those activities on foot of Service Arrangements which provide that they do so in the context of the HSE's statutory obligations to manage and deliver, or arrange to be delivered on its behalf, health and personal social services (Recital 2A).  The arrangement also makes clear that incorporated into the funds provided by the HSE to the respondents are the costs of providing the service (clause 4.1): 

   

 '... the funds to be paid by the Executive to the Provider inclusive of all duties, taxes, expenses and other costs associated with or incurred in the provision of the Services shall not exceed the amount specified in Schedule 6 (Funding). ' 

   

 45.   The undisputed evidence (and facts as found by the Tribunal) were that the respondents agreed to provide accommodation, food and support services to the service users at an agreed rate, invoices being raised to reflect the care needs and fees incurred by the respondents in respect of each service user for whom they care.  This represented the totality or near totality of their income.  The monies used by the respondents to discharge these expenses came from the HSE, (or where relevant, TUSLA) and the HSE's funds came from the Exchequer.  On its face, accordingly, the monies used to discharge the expenses incurred by the respondents in carrying out the activity the subject of the Service Arrangements came from the Exchequer and, to that extent, are reasonably described as being ' defrayed ' out of moneys provided by the Exchequer. 

   

 46.   That this is the proper construction of the section is supported by two other considerations.  First, while TE vigorously contested that the provision applied to the respondents and to that extent it strongly disputed that para. 14(b) meant what the respondents said it meant, it was less enthusiastic when it came to committing itself to what it contended the provision was apt to cover.  Eventually, reflecting a point it made in its written submissions, and having been directly asked that question in case management, it proposed that expenses would be ' defrayed ' by the HSE if the expenses were submitted to it, and then signed off by it before being discharged.  Its emphatic assertion that this was what ' defrayal ' in its ordinary usage meant was noticeably unsupported by authority, or any evident demand of purpose or context.  There was never any evidence that the Health Boards or the HSE ever engaged in processes of this kind. 

   

 47.   Second, following the decision in Glendale , para. 14(b) was amended by the inclusion of the words 'other than a body in relation to which such defrayal occurs by reason of the Nursing Homes Support Scheme Act 2009 '.   There are, of course, two ways of looking at the effect of the addition of these words.  One is to acknowledge that the intention was to copper-fasten the decision in Glendale (which was, of course, one of the High Court), and to guard against the prospect that the Court of Appeal and/or this Court would reach a different conclusion.  But the provision did not, as is customary, express itself to be ' for the avoidance of doubt ', and even without using that formula the same effect could have been achieved by simply providing that nothing in the Schedule should be interpreted as exempting properties which afforded care to those availing of the 2009 Act.  Yet by framing the amendment as it did, the Oireachtas has confirmed the construction of ' defray ' urged by the respondents, and has rendered the argument advanced by TE even more difficult than it already was.  If ' defrayal ' bore the meaning contended for by TE, the reference to the 2009 Act is wholly unnecessary.  Read literally, the provision as it now stands can only mean that what occurred when funding was provided by the State for the provision of nursing home care in accordance with the 2009 Act - as indeed described by Birmingham J. in Glendale - was, in fact, a defrayal of the service provider's expenses in providing the relevant service.  If this was a ' defrayal ' of those provider's expenses, then what occurred in the case of the respondents a fortiori fell within that description. 

   

 *****      

 48.   TE makes, essentially, six points in response.  First, it says that Schedule 4, read as a whole, reflects the clear policy of the Oireachtas to limit exemptions to properties and uses ' that serve a public, charitable, or community-orientated function, and which are not operated for private profit' .  Exemptions, it says, are generally reserved for uses that advance the public good, provide essential social services, or support cultural, educational or community development, rather than for commercial or profit driven enterprises.  The intention, it says, is to support organisations that relieve the State of certain public burdens or provide essential services to the community, rather than to subsidise private enterprises, even where those enterprises provide valuable services. Thus, it rhetorically asks, why should a struggling pharmacy, GP practice or a private nursing home which cares for the elderly pay their share of the rates burden, while the respondents do not? 

   

 49.   Second, it is critical of what it says was the trial judge's over-focus on the words ' out of moneys provided ' as they appear in the section, his failure to apply the maxim noscitur a sociis and thus to place those words in their overall context, and what is said to have been his failure to appreciate the meaning of ' the Exchequer '.  This, TE contends, refers to the Central Fund, which would not be used to directly pay the expenses of any activity; the Exchequer provides an allocation of funds from the Central Fund to the HSE, and the phrase ' out of moneys provided' must be read in that context. 

   

 50.   Third, it says that HSE does not directly pay or ' defray ' the respondent's rent, mortgage repayments, the day-to-day running costs of the house, the light or heating costs, or staff costs.  It is not under a contractual obligation to defray any of these expenses.  It says that just because the price of a service or good is selected in order to cover the costs and profit, does not mean that the purchaser of the product or the service is providing money to defray the expenses of providing that product or service.  If the State was defraying the expenses of a private company, one would expect for those expenses to be submitted and vouched as part of the process by which the payments are made.  The whole point of the Service Arrangement, it says, is that the Exchequer is not responsible for the expenses of the respondents or any individual for-profit service provider. 

   

 51.   Fourth, it argues that the word ' defray ' - the dictionary definition of which it notes is to pay out, discharge an expense, meet the expenses of, or pay the charges or expenses of, or reimburse - has a formality accompanying its meaning.  It says that it is a word associated with expenses or cost , not income or remuneration, and that it is not a word used typically for the payment of a service.  It contends that the construction accepted by the trial judge and urged by the respondents, would involve the interpolation of words into the provision: 

   

   

 ' a body the expenses incurred by which in carrying on an activity as aforesaid are defrayed by that body wholly or mainly out of moneys provided to that body by the Exchequer '. 

   

 52.   Fifth, TE relies upon parts of the judgment of Birmingham J. in Glendale , arguing that these show that the Court must determine whether it can legitimately be said that the expenses of the respondents are being defrayed by the HSE.  If the logic of the High Court judge in this case were applied to Glendale , it argues, the exemption would have been granted because the expenses of the nursing home were being defrayed out of monies provided by the Oireachtas via the individual elderly person entitled to the funding. 

   

 53.   Sixth, and finally, it invokes the principle applied in Nangles Nurseries which it argues makes it clear that exemptions in the 2001 Act are to be interpreted strictly against the ratepayer and ambiguities - if they are found in an exemption - are to be interpreted against the ratepayer.  Here, it contends that the provision is unclear, that it bears the construction urged by TE, and that any ambiguity in the section should be construed against the respondents. 

   

   

 ***** 

   

 54.   The difficulty with these arguments is not merely that they depend on interpolation into the statutory language, but that they do not present any reason of context or purpose for so doing.  The linguistic argument might enjoy greater force if the section referred to costs being defrayed by the HSE, because that language would suggest some direct, specific and formal action by the HSE vis-à-vis the expenses, whether by discharging them directly or by the expenses in question being submitted to the HSE and vouched or approved by it, or by attaching another formal step in the process of payment.  This, however, is not what the provision states.  Rather than envisaging any such interaction, para. 14(b) speaks passively of the expenses being discharged ' out of moneys provided by the Exchequer '.  The section is focussed only on the source of the monies used to pay the expenses, not the identity of the person that incurs, directly discharges or sanctions them.  Its terms are broad and while it would certainly include situations in which the HSE pays the expenses directly, the section is not so limited .  Indeed, for that reason, the construction of the provision does not at all, as suggested by TE, require that the words ' that body ' be read into the section. 

   

 55.   Moreover, it is emphatically not the case that Schedule 4 is concerned only with those providing services in the public interest to the community other than for profit.  In fact, paras. 8 and 14 are conspicuous in that paras. 8(b) and 14(b) are, in practical terms, likely to arise for consideration only when the body providing the services in question is established or conducting its affairs with a view to making a private profit.  The contrast with para. 10, where it is specifically stated that the undertaking not be conducting its business for private profit in order to avail of the exemption, is stark.  It must be inferred that the Oireachtas understood that the Health Boards and later the HSE outsourced some services it was required by law to provide, to private profit-making undertakings.  There is, as I have explained, some reason why when properties owned by such bodies were wholly or largely providing services to the HSE they should enjoy the same exemption from rates as the HSE would if it provided the services from its own property.  There is no evident reason why it would limit the exemption to cases in which the HSE either checked and vouched the expenses, or had a list of expenses provided and those and only those comprised the contract price, or paid the expenses directly itself.  If there was such a reason, it was not identified in this case.  Counsel for TE indeed, fairly accepted that they could not identify any example in which the HSE discharged expenses in this way. 

   

 56.   The amendment to para. 14(b) made following the decision in Glendale renders the question of whether that case was correctly decided, academic.  That said, and apart from the fact that  as the Tribunal in both cases said, and as Bradley J. found - Birmingham J. was concerned with a different statutory regime to that under consideration here, the basis for his conclusion that the State and the HSE in operating the subvention in issue there were defraying the expenses of the individual patient, but not that of the service providers, is not clear to me.  The assumption that it had to be one or the other appears to me to be, at least, questionable.  This is particularly so if the correct approach to the provision required, as Birmingham J. correctly concluded, that the question of whether there was a ' defrayal ' had to be viewed objectively. 

   

 57.   Finally, the emphasis placed by TE on the principle of strict construction falls to be considered in the light of this.  It is not the case that this principle eschews considerations of context and purpose, functioning only to demand that if two ' literal ' constructions of a provision are available, that most favourable to the taxpayer (in the case of a charging provision), or the revenue authorities (in the case of an exemption) must, without further inquiry, be applied.  This, indeed, was observed by Henchy J. in the course of his judgment in Inspector of Taxes v. Kiernan [1981] IR 117 (at p. 121) in a passage cited by MacMenamin J. in Nangles Nurseries : 

   

   

 ' A word or expression in a given statute must be given meaning and scope according to its immediate context, in line with the scheme and purpose of the particular statutory pattern as a whole, and to an extent that will truly effectuate the particular legislation or a particular definition therein. ' 

   

 58.   The consequence was explained by McKechnie J. in the course of his judgment in The People (DPP) v. TN [2020] IESC 26 , at para. 119: 

   

 ' The principle does not mean that whenever two potentially plausible readings of a statute are available, the court must automatically adopt the interpretation which favours the accused; it does not mean that where the defendant can point to any conceivable uncertainty or doubt regarding the meaning of the section, he is entitled to a construction which benefits him.  Rather, it means that where ambiguity should remain following the utilisation of the other approaches and principles of interpretation at the Court's disposal, the accused will then be entitled to the benefit of that ambiguity.  The task for the Court, however, remains the ascertainment of the intention of the legislature through, in the first instance, the application of the literal approach to statutory interpretation. 

   

 59.   That case, obviously, concerned a criminal statute.  The principles were explained in their application to a taxing statute in Bookfinders Ltd. v. Revenue Commissioners [2020] IESC 60 at para. 54: 

   

 ' The general principles of statutory interpretation are tools used to achieve a clear understanding of a statutory provision.  It is only if, after that process has been concluded, a court is genuinely in doubt as to the imposition of a liability, that the principle against doubtful penalisation should apply and the text construed given a strict construction so as to prevent a fresh and unfair imposition of liability by the use of oblique or slack language. ' 

                                                    

 60.   In this case, the application of the principle of strict construction of taxing statutes in general, as applied to exemptions in particular, does not generate any great difficulty. The construction of para. 14(b) urged by the respondents is the literal construction, it has a rationale, and it follows from what I have said that TE has not proposed any plausible alternative construction.  Insofar as it suggests a narrowing of the meaning of the word ' defray ' so that it is limited to a formal process of vouching of expenses, it has not identified any basis in the context or purpose of the 2001 Act for such a limitation (even if the language of para. 14(b) could bear that construction).  But it must be stressed that the effect of these authorities is that it is not sufficient for TE to posit that the interpretation it urges fits within the literal construction of the provision and to propose from there that because this is an exempting provision, it must be construed in accordance with that interpretation.  The requirement that a rule of strict construction is engaged when a provision is shown to give rise to an ambiguity following the application of ' the other approaches and principles of interpretation ' demands that the court also take account of considerations of context and purpose in appraising whether an interpretation is sufficiently plausible to result in an ambiguity.  Viewed that way, the interpretation urged by TE does not give rise to any ambiguity so as to engage principles of strict construction.  Instead, the approach it urges falls foul of the following observation in Bookfinders Ltd. v. Revenue Commissioners (at para. 47): 

   

             ' However, that should not be understood to mean that the interpretation of tax statutes cannot have regard to the purpose of the provision in particular, or that the manner in which the court must approach a taxation statute is to look solely at the words, with or without the aid of a dictionary, and on the basis of that conclude that, if another meaning is capable of being wrenched from the words taken alone, the provision must be treated as ambiguous, and the taxpayer given the benefit of the more beneficial reading. Such an approach can only greatly enhance the prospects of an interpretation which defeats the statutory objective, which is, generally speaking, the antithesis of statutory interpretation. ' 

   

 ***** 

   

 61.   One other matter was addressed by Birmingham J. in the course of his judgment in Glendale .  There, a question presented in the case stated raised an issue as to the meaning of the phrase ' wholly or mainly ' as it appeared in para. 14(b) (' the expenses incurred by which ... are defrayed wholly or mainly out of moneys ').  The ratepayer contended that ' mainly ' meant anything more than 50%, while the Commissioner - relying upon a decision of the Court of Appeal for England and Wales in R v. Radio Authority, ex parte Bull and anor. [1997] 3 WLR 1094 (' ex parte Bull' ) contended that it meant more than 75%.  In that case, the Court of Appeal decided that the phrase ' wholly or mainly ' when used in the context of a prohibition on the broadcast of advertisements by bodies whose objects were ' wholly or mainly of a political nature ' should by reason of the considerations of freedom of communication involved, be construed restrictively.  Lord Woolf MR explained (at p. 1103): 

   

 ' "Wholly or mainly" is a phrase the meaning of which is not free from ambiguity. Clearly it requires a proportion which is more than half.  But how much more?  51 per cent. or 99 per cent. and anything between are candidates. ' 

   

 62.   That language, should, he said, be construed as applicable only to bodies whose objects were substantially or primarily political; a body to come within the provision, Lord Woolf said, ' must be at least midway between the two percentages I have identified, i.e. more than 75 per cent. ' 

   

 63.   In Glendale , Birmingham J. rejected this construction of the phrase as it was used in para. 14(b), differentiating the human rights related issue in ex parte Bull from the question of measuring how costs or expenses are defrayed.  In the latter case, he reasoned, ' a more mathematical approach ' was required, and that meant that if there was evidence to establish that more than 50% of the expenses of a body are defrayed from a particular source, it was proper to say that those expenses were mainly so defrayed (para. 34). 

   

 64.   I disagree with the approach adopted by Birmingham J. to this aspect of para. 14(b) which, respectfully, underplays the basis for the exemption in the first place.  In settling on the correct meaning of the term ' wholly or mainly ' as it is used in this provision, it is necessary to look to the reason the paragraph was introduced.  As I have explained, the objective was to extend an exemption to those private operators providing services to the HSE (or, where relevant, other state agency) where the services, if delivered from a property by the HSE itself, would give rise to an exemption from rates for the HSE.  The reason for the exemption was that without it, the HSE would end up indirectly discharging the rates even though the evident legislative policy was that it should not pay rates in respect of premises from which it provided such services itself.  Thus, the provision was concerned to identify properties that, although run privately and for profit, are functionally equivalent to properties owned and operated by the HSE (or, where relevant, other state agency) because they both provide services that are public in nature, and are funded in doing so by the State.  For that reason, the word ' mainly ' as it appears in para. 14(b) must be understood in conjunction with ' wholly ' .  If the provision only used the word ' wholly ' there would be the potential for injustice because only a facility which derived 100% of its income from the State could benefit from the exemption.  To construe the phrase so that 49%, or for that matter 24%, of the business of such a facility could come from private sources and yet still enjoy the exemption would not only be inconsistent with that rationale, but would also confer a potentially significant competitive advantage on undertakings which took some public patients but still derived a substantial portion of their income from private sources, over those who derived less of their income from the State.  The legislature did not use a mathematical formula to describe this, and for that reason it does not seem to me to be correct for the court to invent and impose one.  But the intent was quite clear: care facilities of the kind referred to in para. 14 all, or effectively all, of the expenses of which are discharged by the Exchequer are exempt.  This allows for some tolerance where there is a small contribution to those expenses looked at on an overall basis from fees paid by private patients (as would occur for example if there were occasional private patients), or perhaps from donations, but the level of that contribution would have to be such that an informed lay bystander would say that 'for all intents and purposes', the expenses of the facility in question are discharged by the Exchequer. That is the case in these appeals.  

   

 65.   For the foregoing reasons, this appeal should be dismissed, and the questions presented in each case stated answered as proposed by Bradley J..  Based upon the findings of the Tribunal in each case, the properties of the respondents the subject of these appeals are relevant property not rateable by reason of para. 14(b) of Schedule 4 to the 2001 Act.
